phase: tier 5 done (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus × 3, no README), post-run review clean
findings: Tier 5 (19.2k lines of Rust, nine more extension layers, built so that a site's content follows mechanically from the docs once found): finding sites did not get hard again for strong models, and the compiler still rescues the weak one. 22 of 108 runs pass: Haiku Rust 1/18 vs Python 0/18, Sonnet 4/18 vs 3/18, Opus 10/18 vs 4/18 (p ≈ 0.09; all models 15/54 vs 7/54, p ≈ 0.09). A per-site analysis of every run's diff splits the failures. Sites the compiler flags (outside between_in, where a parser rewrite meant no new node existed): Rust 0 misses in 45 runs. Python missed at least one in 6/15 Haiku runs, 2/15 Sonnet runs and 0/15 Opus runs; Haiku at tier 3 was 6/18. Sites nothing flags were missed in both languages, with Python missing more (Rust 41, Python 62). Those include lint through the simple-CASE expansion (18/18 missed), BETWEEN/IN and NOT LIKE rewritten in the parser, ALTER missing from the change log, and the DESCRIBE typing rules. Tracing every cell where Rust and Python differ, the compiler's net contribution to passes is about zero. It rescued one Haiku run and cost two Sonnet runs, where its forced JSON arms got wrong content that Python's fallback got right. The rest of the +8 gap comes from three sources. A test-suite asymmetry (+3): a Python-only unit test pins the list of change kinds, and Python agents cite it as their reason not to record ALTER in the change log. Possibly Option making the unknown case visible in DESCRIBE (+2, Opus date, unverified). Silent sites and content (+4), which looks like chance at n = 3. A post-run review found no test faults and four small base asymmetries that cut both ways.

Tier 4 (12.5k lines of Rust, 7 more extension layers, identical docs in both languages): the type system no longer decides anything for any model. After a post-run audit of the hidden tests, 20 of 108 runs pass: Haiku Rust 2/18 vs Python 1/18, Sonnet 3/18 vs 2/18, Opus 8/18 vs 4/18 (p ≈ 0.29). Nearly every failure is at a site no type checks, and it fails in both languages: lint rules applied through BETWEEN/IN and simple-CASE expansions (0 of 36 runs), DESCRIBE typing of date arithmetic (1 of 18), the ALTER view-dependency check, BETWEEN/IN and NOT LIKE rewritten in the parser. Python agents reached the sites Rust's compiler names: only 1 of 54 Python runs crashed at an unhandled variant (Haiku at tier 3: 6 of 18). The codebase is consistent enough that grepping for a sibling variant finds the same list the compiler gives. Rust's forced arms again came with wrong content, e.g. DATE written as a plain JSON string: Rust right in 3 of 9 runs, Python 9 of 9, through its generic fallback. Reading: at scale, the bottleneck is the semantic rules, not finding the sites, and types only help with finding the sites.

Experiment 1 across three models: the compiler's advantage is a weak-model effect. With the README's extension docs removed (code unchanged), 3 repeats × 6 tasks per cell: Haiku Rust 10/18 vs Python 5/18, and 6 of 18 Python runs missed a site Rust's compiler flags (Rust 0, p ≈ 0.02). Sonnet 11/18 vs 12/18, and Opus 18/18 vs 13/18: neither missed a single compiler-flagged site in Python (0 of 36). Sonnet and Opus found the JSON writers and the hand-written serialization on their own. Their Python failures are all at sites no type checks (BETWEEN/IN kept as a parser expansion, the optional COLUMN in ALTER digests). The ALTER one is partly a documentation confound: the Rust digest module states "optional words are left out" as a rule, while the Python docstring only implies it. Meanwhile exhaustive matching cut the other way for Rust: 5 Rust runs (Haiku 2, Sonnet 3) added the forced arm with the wrong content, e.g. a JSON import arm for DATE that reads a plain string, where Python's generic fallback handled the typed form automatically. Reading: types tell you where, not what. That matters for a weak agent that can't find the where on its own, and stops mattering once the agent can.

Tier 3: types tell you where, not what. I added four extension layers to toydb (JSON output, statement digests, column statistics, export/import) that consume the core types, so each feature task has to reach code far from where the feature lives. Transplant (tier-2 solutions dropped onto tier 3 unchanged): in Rust, 10 of 12 feature solutions fail to compile, and every error names a missing extension site. In Python, 6 of 12 fail the agent's own visible script (a crash or wrong answers), but 4 (DATE, release) pass the visible script and the entire existing suite while failing every extension script. The remaining 2 per language (BETWEEN/IN) are silent in both. Real agents on tier 3 didn't need the compiler for this: Python agents reached every site Rust's compiler would have flagged, in 12 of 12 feature runs (the README's Extensions section names them). Of the 7 failures (Rust 3, Python 4, all escaped with a green check.sh), every one is at a site no type system in either language checks: digest text, JSON member lists, statistics upkeep, and whether BETWEEN stays in the AST.

First spread, at tier 2, and it says something about where types help. 2 of the 5 tier-1 Haiku Python solutions to the feature tasks (CASE, DATE) pass every tier-1 test and the whole tier-2 suite when applied unchanged to the full codebase, then crash on the cluster wire (UnexpectedEof). Python's hand-written serialization was skipped or incomplete. At tier 1 nothing uses it, so it looks like dead code. Rust: 0 such failures of 10, because serde is derived. Python Opus: 0 of 5. Agents working on the full codebase got it right in Python too, 12 of 12 with or without a hint: there the README and the code show that values and plans cross the network. Reading: types (here, derived serialization) protect weak agents when the code that consumes a change is out of their view. That is what tier 3 is built to test.

Tier 1 (toydb SQL core, about 6k lines) still shows no spread: 27 of 28 runs pass. The one failure is Haiku in Python on DISTINCT, an escaped defect: COUNT(DISTINCT) gives the argument-count error instead of the parse error the spec gives twice. Rust costs Haiku about 12% more output tokens (geometric mean over tasks) and Opus nothing; turns are level. Compile time is negligible: 59–62 s of Rust builds across 7 tasks against roughly 2,000–2,400 s of wall time.
design: Subject: toydb (Erik Grinaker, Apache-2.0) and a structurally parallel Python port that passes the same golden scripts byte for byte. Each tier is a larger slice of it: SQL core (tier 1), full toydb with Raft (tier 2), and extension layers that consume the core types (tiers 3–4).
Arms: Rust (compiler + one visible golden script + check.sh) vs Python (the same visible script + check.sh, no type checker).
Agents: Claude Code subagents with a fixed prompt: Haiku · low, Sonnet · medium and Opus · high.
Correctness: hidden golden scripts (SQL and end-to-end cluster scripts), compared byte for byte, plus the full regression suite (every existing golden script and unit test).

Oracle: an author writes each task's spec and hidden scripts; two independent reference implementations, one per language, must agree byte for byte, and a reconciler settles every disagreement against the spec.
isolation: Each run gets its own workspace: the tier's codebase, TASK.md, one visible golden script and check.sh.
The prompt forbids reading outside the workspace, using the web and spawning subagents. Every Bash/Read/Grep path in each transcript is audited afterwards.
Hidden scripts, reference solutions and other runs' workspaces are chmod 000 while agents run.
The Rust build is pre-warmed, so the agent never pays the cold dependency build.
Hidden scripts are copied into the workspace only at grading time, and the task directories are restored afterwards.
metrics: Pass: build OK, every hidden golden script matches byte for byte, and the full regression suite stays green.
Escaped defects: last visible check green but hidden tests fail. This is the headline number for the talk.
Effort: turns, tool calls, output/thinking tokens and input tokens incl. cache, all from subagent transcripts (deduplicated per API message).
Time: total wall time, plus time inside check.sh split into build and tests (logged by check.sh itself), so time excluding compile is exact.
Validator signal: how many check.sh runs, and how many failed at compile vs failed visible tests.
next: Where this leaves the talk. Tier 3: the compiler rescued a weak model that couldn't find the consumers of a change. Tier 4: in a larger, consistent codebase every model in both languages finds the consumers (by grep if not by compiler) and fails on rules no type expresses. Tier 5 (19k lines): the same split holds at nearly twice the size. The weak model misses compiler-flagged sites in Python (6/15 runs) and never in Rust, while strong models find them either way, and everyone fails on silent semantic rules. Types tell you where, not what. Past a certain codebase quality, the where is only the bottleneck for weak models.
Possible cheap follow-ups: a with-README tier-5 arm (does documentation fix the silent semantic misses?); a pyright arm for Python; more Opus repeats at tier 5 to test the 10/18 vs 4/18 gap.
scale_plan: Reference codebase: toydb (Erik Grinaker, Apache-2.0). A distributed SQL database in Rust: lexer/parser, planner with 5 optimizers, executor, MVCC transactions, bitcask/memory storage, key encoding, Raft. It is about 7.9k lines of non-test code (+3.8k inline tests) and ships 107 golden test scripts for SQL and storage, with about 10k lines of expected output in a language-neutral command → output format, including 428 exact error messages and printed plan trees.

Port direction: Rust → Python. The Rust original is the trusted reference, and its golden scripts become the acceptance test for the Python port: a Python goldenscript runner plus ports of toydb's test runners. A port that passes all 107 scripts byte for byte is behaviourally equivalent, which avoids the problem of having to trust AI-written Python.

Tier 1 (done, 2026-11-17: 27/28 pass): toydb SQL core in-process: parser, types, planner/optimizer, executor, local engine, MVCC, storage, encoding. About 6.2k lines of Rust application code against 7.8k lines in the Python port. A pipeline of 7 Fable 5.2 agents built the port in 57 minutes (1.29M tokens). It passes 130/130 golden-script runs byte for byte (93 SQL plus 37 storage) and 117 unit tests, which I re-checked myself. An independent Fable reviewer found it faithful with no cheating; the issues it raised were minor, e.g. the sorted-list BTreeMap is O(n) per insert.

Tier 2 (done, 2026-11-18: 28/28 pass; transplant test shows 2 silent Python Haiku failures): full toydb, adding Raft consensus, the Raft SQL engine, server/client, bins and the end-to-end cluster tests. About 8.5k lines of Rust and 11.3k of Python application code.

Tier 3 (done, 2026-11-19: Rust 11/14, Python 10/14; every failure at a site no type checks; transplant: Rust's compiler flags 10/12 tier-2 solutions, Python's own checks 6/12): tier 2 plus four extension layers, JSON output, statement digests, column statistics, export/import, about 1.5k lines per language. The extensions are consumers of the core types (Value, DataType, plan nodes, AST, catalog), so the same tasks must also reach code far from the SQL core.

The same 7 tasks at every tier, so only the codebase size changes:
  • between_in, a local control.
  • case, which touches expression traversal, aggregates and folding.
  • date, a new type that touches every match on Value/DataType and the order of the key encoding.
  • distinct, including DISTINCT aggregates.
  • alter: ADD, DROP and RENAME COLUMN, which need backfill and index re-keying, and Raft catalog writes at tier 2.
  • release: six small changes in six areas.
  • bugfix: four injected logic bugs, as a control.

Oracle for the new tasks: a Fable 5.2 / Opus 5.5 author writes the SPEC, a visible script and 8–12 hidden golden scripts. Two independent Fable 5.2 implementers, one per language, see only the SPEC and the visible script. A reconciler then makes both references pass every hidden script byte for byte, logging any spec amendment, and checks that the hidden scripts fail on the unmodified base.
tier1: Setup: 7 tasks × Rust/Python × Haiku-low/Opus-high, one agent at a time. Each workspace is a copy of the tier-1 crate or package, with TASK.md (the spec plus how to work), one visible golden script and an instrumented check.sh. Grading uses 9–13 hidden golden scripts per task plus the whole existing suite.
Correctness: 27/28 pass, 323/324 hidden scripts. Every regression suite stays green. The one failure (Haiku, Python, distinct) is an escaped defect: the agent's last check.sh was green.

Effort: Haiku uses about 2.5× Opus's output tokens and about 1.7× its turns in both languages. Rust vs Python, per task: Haiku's output tokens are 0.84–1.48× (geometric mean 1.12×), Opus's 0.84–1.24× (1.01×); turns 1.03× and 0.87×.

Time: agents ran check.sh only 1–6 times per run. A Rust check averages about 3 s of incremental build (at most 10 s) plus 1.7 s of tests; a Python check spends about 5 s in its test suite. So total validator time is slightly lower in Rust: about 90 s against 105 s across 7 tasks. Without validator time, wall time is within 15% between the languages.
Isolation: no out-of-workspace reads. The audit flagged two paths, both the harness's saved copies of the agent's own oversized tool outputs (its TASK.md and planner.py).

Reading: a 6k-line codebase still fits comfortably in a strong or weak agent's working view, and the tasks are well specified, so tier 1 sits at the ceiling. Tier 2 nearly doubles the code (Raft, server, client) and makes ALTER reach the Raft catalog path.
tier2: Setup: the same 7 tasks and 28 cells on the full codebase. Hidden tests are the tier-1 SQL scripts plus 3–4 cluster scripts per task (real 3–5 node clusters, several clients). TASK.md says that cluster scripts are among the hidden tests.
Correctness: 28/28 pass, every cluster script included. 20 of 28 agents wrote a cluster script of their own; the hint invited this.

Effort: about as at tier 1. Rust/Python output tokens are 0.91× for Haiku and 0.99× for Opus (geometric mean per task), turns 0.92× and 0.97×. Wall time rose 35–57%, mostly because a check now takes about 20 s instead of 7 s. Validator time is now larger in Python: about 440 s against Rust's 330 s for Haiku, and 425 s against 500 s for Opus, whose Rust runs include more full rebuilds.

Where the tasks reach at tier 2 (the reference builders' analysis): new expression, plan-node and aggregate variants travel in Raft scan filters and EXPLAIN results, and new values travel in rows and schemas. Rust derives all of this; Python's encoders are hand-written next to the types. ALTER needs a new Raft command in both languages. The Rust compiler forces it; in Python, a missing catalog method makes ALTER on a cluster silently do nothing.

Isolation: no reads outside the workspace. Two Haiku agents wrote scratch scripts one directory above their workspace and deleted them; the other flags are the harness's saved copies of agents' own outputs.
transplant: Each tier-1 run's final diff applied unchanged to the tier-2 base. Every file a tier-1 agent edited is byte-identical at tier 2. The diff is then graded with the tier-2 hidden scripts. Tier-1 agents had no hint and no test reaching the cluster paths, so this asks whether a solution that is green on the small codebase is correct in the big one.

Silent failures (all of tier 2's existing suite green, cluster scripts fail): Python Haiku on CASE and DATE, where requests carrying the new expression or value can't be decoded (UnexpectedEof). Rust: none of the 10 feature-task transplants. Python Opus: none.

Not counted: DISTINCT (Python Haiku) fails only on how EXPLAIN prints Distinct, which tier 1 left unspecified (the tier-2 addendum fixes it), plus its known tier-1 bug. ALTER fails in all four transplants by design, because it needs a Raft command. The failure is loud in both languages: a Rust compile error, or 6 existing Python cluster tests breaking.
nohint: 16 Haiku runs at tier 2 with TASK.md not saying that cluster scripts are graded: CASE, DATE, DISTINCT and RELEASE, Rust and Python, 2 repeats each.

15/16 pass; every cluster script that depends on serialization passes. All 8 Python agents changed the hand-written serialization, including the 4 that wrote no cluster test of their own. So the hint was not what made tier 2 safe.

The one failure (Python, DISTINCT, repeat b) is the same escaped defect as tier 1's Python Haiku run: COUNT(DISTINCT) gives the argument-count error. That is now 2 of 4 Python Haiku DISTINCT runs against 0 of 4 in Rust. It is a parser error-ordering slip, not a type error.
Isolation: two Rust agents listed the parent runs/ directory (which shows the names of sibling workspaces) while cleaning up scratch files they had written there. No other workspace was read.
tier3: Setup. Tier 2 plus four extension layers, about 1.5k lines each in Rust and Python, written to one language-neutral spec by independent agents and reconciled to byte-identical output on 32 extension scripts. Each extension follows generic rules: plan JSON is derived from the display, digests are canonical SQL with literals as ?, statistics follow their columns, and import goes through INSERT. So the correct output for a new construct follows from the spec without naming it. Python follows the port's case _: panic convention, so a missed arm fails loudly at run time rather than silently.

Hidden scripts: each task's tier-1 and tier-2 scripts, plus 5–6 new extension scripts (SQL and cluster) per feature task that drive the feature through the extensions. TASK.md is the same as at tier 2 and doesn't mention the extensions; agents learn about them only from the README.
Result: Rust 11/14, Python 10/14 (Haiku 5/7 vs 4/7, Opus 6/7 vs 6/7). All 7 failures passed the agent's own last check.sh. Per task:

· between_in (Rust Opus, Python Haiku): BETWEEN/IN still expanded in the parser, as at tiers 1–2, so SHOW STATEMENTS shows v >= ? AND v <= ? and merges it with the hand-written expansion. Rust Haiku and Python Opus kept the constructs in the AST. Neither type system can force this.

· alter (Rust Haiku, both Python): the digest keeps the optional COLUMN (ADD COLUMN x), although EXT_SPEC §3.2 says optional words are left out, including for statements added later. Rust Haiku also didn't move or drop column statistics on RENAME/DROP. The compiler forces a digest arm but not its text.
· release (Rust Haiku): NOT LIKE is lowered in the parser, so its digest reads NOT s LIKE ?. Silent in both languages.
· distinct (Python Haiku): the JSON for the Distinct node carries an extra width member; the spec says nodes carry only what their display line shows. A Rust agent could make the same mistake.

Cost: Rust Haiku used 23% more output tokens than Python Haiku (573k vs 465k over 7 tasks) and about 18% more wall time. For Opus the two are level (236k vs 241k tokens). Compile time totalled 162–221 s per setting, against 590–620 s of Python test time; the Python suite is about 1.6× slower here.

Visible = the agent's own visible script fails; hidden only = every test the agent can run passes. The transplant below confirms this table on the agents' real tier-2 solutions.

transplant3: Each tier-2 run's final changes were applied to a fresh tier-3 base by a per-file three-way merge. 21 of 28 had textual conflicts (adjacent keyword-list entries, keyword-count tests, enum variant numbers). Opus agents resolved them under a rule to keep both sides and add nothing, without building or testing. A script checked that every edit stayed inside a conflict region or was a permitted renumbering. I fixed three resolution errors by hand: two keyword counts were one short, and in the date runs the run's DEFAULT-literal rendering was moved into the display closure, as the reference port does.

Rust: 10 of 12 feature solutions don't build. Every error is a non-exhaustive match or missing field at an extension site, so the compiler lists the work. The two that build are BETWEEN/IN, which then fail all 6 extension scripts silently.

Python: 6 of 12 fail the visible script, so an agent would notice: CASE and ALTER crash in the digest printer, and DISTINCT loses its flag in the AST rewrite. 4 of 12 (DATE, release) pass the visible script and the whole existing suite, then fail all 6 extension scripts. 2 (BETWEEN/IN) are silent as in Rust. Bugfix carries over in both languages (4/4).

So, counting what the agent's own check.sh would flag: Rust 10/12, Python 6/12. This is the same pattern as the tier-1→2 transplant, now on six tasks instead of two: when the consumers of a change are out of the agent's view, Rust's compiler finds them and Python's tests often don't. The real tier-3 runs show the other half: given a README that names the consumers, the weak Python agent found them anyway.
exp1: Setup. Same tier-3 workspaces, task files and hidden tests as above, but each workspace's README is the tier-2 README: accurate for everything except that it doesn't mention the four extensions. The extension code, its comments and its tests are still in the repo, so agents can still find it by exploring. 6 feature tasks × Rust/Python × 3 repeats for each of Haiku-low, Sonnet-medium and Opus-high (108 runs; bugfix has no extension sites). Every failure escaped: the agent's own last check.sh was green.

Missed sites the compiler flags: Haiku Python 6/18, everyone else 0. Haiku: case b, c and release a never added the construct to the JSON writer (crashes only under [json]); distinct b, c: the JSON aggregate writer silently drops DISTINCT; distinct a, c: hand-written Raft serialization drops the flag. In Rust each of these is a non-exhaustive match, a missing field or derived serde (0/18 vs 6/18, p ≈ 0.02). Sonnet and Opus in Python: 0/36.

Right site, wrong content: Rust 5, Python 0. Rust date (Haiku c, Sonnet b, c): the compiler forced a DATE arm in the JSON importer, and the agent wrote it to read a plain string instead of the typed {"type":"DATE",…} form. In the Python base, typed forms of any type go through one generic fallback, so there was nothing to get wrong. Rust distinct (Haiku c: an extra width member; Sonnet c: count(DISTINCT _) in upper case).

Sites no type checks: BETWEEN/IN kept as a parser expansion (Haiku 6/6, Sonnet 5/6, Opus 2/6, both languages); the optional COLUMN kept in ALTER digests (Haiku Rust 1, Python 3; Sonnet Rust 2, Python 3; Opus Rust 0, Python 3); NOT LIKE digests (Haiku only); statistics upkeep (Haiku Python 2, Opus Python 1).

Confound: ALTER digests. The two implementations were written independently, and their digest docs differ. Rust's module comment lists "Optional words are left out (e.g. INNER, OUTER, ASC, TRANSACTION)" as a rule; Python's docstring says statements differing in optional words share a digest. Opus Rust got the ALTER digest right 3/3, Opus Python 0/3. Excluding ALTER, Opus is 15/15 vs 13/15 (p ≈ 0.48). This affects only the no-type-checks bucket, not the missed-site count.

Cost: Sonnet was the cheapest by far (25k output tokens and ~30 turns per run, the same in both languages). Rust cost about 8% more output tokens than Python for Haiku and 4% for Opus, and the same for Sonnet. Python spent 82–104 s per run in tests, Rust 44–51 s plus 17–21 s compiling.
Caveat: n = 3 per cell. The robust results are the Haiku-only missed-site count and its disappearance at Sonnet and Opus; the pass-rate differences per model are within noise apart from Haiku.

tier4: Codebase. Tier 3 plus seven extension layers that consume the core types: FORMAT (canonical SQL), views, DESCRIBE (inferred types and nullability), ESTIMATE (row estimates from statistics), prepared statements with a plan cache, LINT (8 warning rules), and a change log (SHOW CHANGES). Rust application code is 12,498 lines (tier 3: 10,070) and Python 14,930. The 20k target needs a tier 5. Every extension module's doc comments use the same text in both languages, and the tier-3 docs were harmonised too, which removes the ALTER-digest confound of experiment 1.

Tasks. The same 6 feature tasks, each with 6–8 new hidden tier-4 scripts. A tier-3 solution dropped onto tier 4 fails to compile in Rust in every task, and the errors name the formatter, lint, describe, estimate and prepared sites. In Python it mostly crashes there instead (case _: panic), apart from a few silent sites (date DESCRIBE, the distinct formatter). Every task except distinct also has at least one site no type checks in either language.

Setup. The experiment-1 condition: the README is the tier-2 README (no extension docs at all), and the code and its doc comments are unchanged. 6 tasks × Rust/Python × Haiku-low, Sonnet-medium and Opus-high × 3 repeats (108 runs), with the same prompt as tier 3. Isolation audit: clean (5 runs wrote scratch files outside their workspace and deleted them; none read anything outside it). Three Haiku Python runs gave up without changing code.

Post-run test audit. Raw grading gave only 13/108 passes, with several scripts failing uniformly across models, so an Opus auditor checked every script failing in ≥3 runs against what the agents could see (TASK.md, the code and its docs, the tier-2 README). It found no test faults, and 7 underdetermined failure modes that EXT4_SPEC fixed but the agent-visible docs did not: the lint warning count and order for expansions, the NOT LIKE lint message, the DISTINCT estimate rule, and the order of the ALTER view check. These lines were removed or replaced with cases on which every reading agrees; no expected value changed, and each script still fails on the base and passes both references (toydb/tiers/t4/POSTRUN_AMENDMENTS.md). Re-scoring changed 7 runs: 13 → 20. One of them (release Opus Rust c) passes only because the removed lines tested a rule it hadn't implemented, so strictly 19.
tier4_tasks: Lint not applied through the expansion (all 18); BETWEEN/IN rewritten in the parser (15/18, against the digest doc's “constructs are never rewritten”)
Lint not applied through the simple-CASE expansion (all 18); some DESCRIBE/JSON content
DESCRIBE: date plus an operand of unknown type is DATE by the doc's rule (17/18 missed it); Rust Haiku/Sonnet: DATE written as a JSON string (6/6)
Mostly passes; JSON display count(distinct _) casing, extra JSON members

Optional COLUMN kept in FORMAT/digests; no view-dependency check (Rust 5/9 and Python 4/9 implemented it); change log: Rust 8/9 record an alter_table change, Python 0/9 (records the rewritten rows or nothing)
NOT LIKE rewritten to NOT (a LIKE b); NOT LIKE lint rule (Rust 4/9, Python 1/9); DESCRIBE of bool_and over a string
tier4_sites: Sites the compiler names: reached in both languages. Every Rust run compiled, so every forced arm exists. Python agents got there too: 1 of 54 Python runs crashed at an unhandled variant (Sonnet release c: the new functions missing in the tier-3 JSON expression writer). The forced arms are many (describe, lint, format, estimate, prepared, JSON), and the content in them is where the Rust runs failed: DATE as a JSON string (Rust right in 3/9, Python 9/9), COLUMN kept in FORMAT (Rust 2/9 right, Python 3/9).
Sites no type checks: missed in both languages. Lint through expansions 0/36 runs; date DESCRIBE 1/18; the ALTER view check R 5/9, P 4/9; BETWEEN/IN kept in the AST 3/18.

Two silent sites where Rust did better. The ALTER change log (Rust 8/9, Python 0/9) and the NOT LIKE lint rule (Rust 4/9, Python 1/9). Nothing in the types requires either. Correction after tier 5: the change log is mostly a test-suite asymmetry. Python's base has a unit test that pins the list of change kinds (test_kind), and Rust has none. Python runs cite it as their reason not to add an ALTER kind: 3 of 9 at tier 4 and 4 of 9 at tier 5.
Cost. Per run, as at tier 3: Sonnet is cheapest (about 30k output tokens). Rust costs Haiku 33% more output tokens than Python, and costs Sonnet and Opus about the same.
lede: The same codebase in Rust and Python: toydb, a distributed SQL database, at growing sizes (tiers 1–4). Agents of different strength get identical tasks; a compiler (or not) plus a few visible tests are their only validators; held-back tests decide correctness.
tokens: A separate data point from Kimi. In a separate replication, Kimi K3.1 Pro got the same brief. It wrote its own small Rust and Python SQL engines rather than porting toydb, then ran 5 tier-2 feature tasks once per language. Its Rust runs used 4,315,253 tokens against 3,355,082 for Python: +28.6%. Rust cost more on 4 of the 5 tasks; CHECK constraints was the exception. That gap may come from the language's verbosity rather than its types: Kimi's Rust base was 4,041 lines against 2,226 lines of Python (1.8×), so there was more code to read.

In this experiment the gap is small, and it doesn't always favour Python. Across tiers 1–4 the Rust–Python difference in total tokens runs from −7% to +8%. Tier 5 runs the other way: Python used 25% more tokens than Rust (622M against 499M). Haiku and Sonnet took more turns in Python, while Opus came out even. So it isn't a fixed Rust tax. Here the Rust code is shorter than the Python port (tier 2: 8.5k vs 11.3k lines), the opposite of Kimi's ratio. That fits the idea that code size, rather than the type system, drives much of Kimi's gap.
The largest Rust premium was Haiku at tier 4 (+37%). Sonnet and Opus used a little less in Rust at tier 4.

Most tokens are cache reads: each turn resends the conversation so far. So totals track how many turns a run takes, more than how much the model writes. Output tokens alone are noisier but show the same pattern.
tier5: Codebase. Tier 4 plus nine extension layers that consume the core types: users and privileges, an audit log, CHECK constraints, row-level security policies, a PostgreSQL wire protocol, backups, system tables, materialized views and query profiles. Rust application code is 19,233 lines (tier 4: 12,498); Python is 20,709. The layers were designed to be mechanical: once an agent finds a site, what goes there follows from the module's documented rule. That isolates finding sites from getting their content right.

Tasks and setup. The same 6 tasks, each with 9–22 new hidden tier-5 scripts (83 in all), plus the tier-2 to tier-4 hidden scripts. The condition is the experiment-1/tier-4 one: the tier-2 README, with code and doc comments unchanged. That gives 108 runs (6 tasks × 2 languages × Haiku-low, Sonnet-medium, Opus-high × 3). The runs went in two lanes, one Rust and one Python agent at a time, so wall times are not comparable with tier 4. Tokens and turns are.

Test audits. A pre-run audit re-derived every expected line from the agent-visible material and found 0 faults and 1 underdetermined line, which was removed. After the runs, four Opus reviewers checked the bases (users…pgwire; backup…profile) and the hidden tests (three tasks each). All 12 reference solutions pass every hidden script with byte-identical output across languages. Baselines, line counts, doc parity and about 1,000 cross-language probe statements check out. No test faults, no regrades, no reruns.

Base asymmetries the review found change effort, not expected output, and cut both ways. Favouring Python: in Python, adding a keyword turns three existing keyword tests red, which points at the keyword-category site; in Rust it stays silent. Also favouring Python: date's pgwire and backup-tag sites are automatic in Python. Favouring Rust: release's owner-kept rule sits in one Rust helper against three inline Python checks, and alter's constraint naming already exists in Rust. The per-site data shows the keyword hint made no measurable difference (Python missed the category 4 times in between_in, Rust 2).

Isolation. Clean: no run read hidden tests, references or other runs. The session scratchpad, which held old tier-2/3 working files, was found unlocked mid-run, because the harness tells every subagent about it and 36 runs used it as a temp directory. No run read a file that predates the runs; one Haiku run listed its file names and opened none of them. Seven Haiku runs wrote scratch files outside their workspace; all were cleaned up. One Haiku run (date, Python, a) ended while its own check was still running, and is graded as left.
tier5_tasks: BETWEEN/IN rewritten in the parser (Rust 8/9, Python 7/9): digests, FORMAT, lint and stored view/CHECK/policy text show the expansion. Neither language flags it. The 3 runs that kept the nodes reached every forced site.

Lint rules through the simple-CASE expansion missed by all 18. Rust: forced sites with wrong content (pg name ?column? for case, DESCRIBE). Python Haiku/Sonnet: 8 loud-at-use sites (JSON, DESCRIBE) never exercised, so missed.

Backup stores the day count instead of the display string (Rust 6/9, Python 5/9; Opus 0). DESCRIBE with an unknown operand is DATE (only Rust Opus 3/3 right; Python 8/9 wrong). Rust Sonnet wrote DATE as a plain JSON string, a site automatic in Python.
Rust missed no site. Python Haiku missed 8 (digest printer, JSON aggregate writer, the formatter's SELECT DISTINCT). Content: extra JSON members, count(DISTINCT _) casing.
ALTER missing from the change log (Python 9/9, Rust 5/9). Haiku: view, matview and CHECK/policy dependency checks. FORMAT/digests keep the optional COLUMN.
NOT LIKE rewritten to NOT (a LIKE b) (Rust 3/9, all Haiku; Python 5/9). DESCRIBE type of bool_and/bool_or wrong in 11/18 (Haiku 6/6, Sonnet 5/6, Opus 0/6), at a site every run reached.
tier5_sites: Method. Six Opus analysts classified every site of every run from the agent's diff against the baseline commit, checked against the failing scripts' diffs. Each site was marked reached correctly (by an edit, or automatically by the base), reached with wrong content, missed, or not applicable. That is 3,312 site-runs over 6 tasks; files in reviews/t5/sites_*.{json,md}.

Sites the Rust compiler flags. Leaving out between_in, where 15 of 18 runs rewrote the construct in the parser, so no new AST node existed for the compiler to flag: Rust missed 0 in 45 runs. Python missed at least one in 6/15 Haiku runs (14 sites), 2/15 Sonnet runs (5) and 0/15 Opus runs. Python's misses were sites that crash at first use but that the agents' own tests never exercised: the JSON writers, DESCRIBE, the digest printer, the formatter. In Rust, the forced sites then had wrong content 44 times (Haiku 23, Sonnet 21, Opus 0), against Python's 34 (23, 10, 1).

Sites nothing flags. Missed in both languages: Rust 41 (Haiku 24, Sonnet 8, Opus 9), Python 62 (35, 15, 12), between_in excluded. These are lint through the simple-CASE expansion (18/18), the change-log entry for ALTER (Rust 5/9, Python 9/9), the DESCRIBE typing rules, and the alter dependency checks. Rust also missed fewer of these sites, which no type checks. The biggest single source is the ALTER change-log entry. Python's base has a unit test (test_kind) that pins the list of change kinds, and Rust has no equivalent, since a Rust test can't enumerate enum variants. Python agents cite it as the reason they recorded nothing: 4 runs at tier 5 and 3 at tier 4.

Answer to the tier-5 question. At ~20k lines, finding sites did not get hard again for Sonnet and Opus. No Opus run in either language missed a site the compiler names; their failures are at silent semantic sites and wrong content. For Haiku it looks like tier 3 again: the compiler takes Rust Haiku to every flagged site, and Python Haiku misses them in 6 of 15 runs (Rust 0/15, p ≈ 0.02). It does not make Haiku pass, though: Rust Haiku filled those sites with wrong content and passed 1 of 18.

Did the pass gap come from the type system? Mostly not. Each cell where Rust and Python pass counts differ was traced to the sites that decided it (reviews/t5/ATTRIBUTION.md). Compiler-checked types: +1 −2. The +1 is a Haiku distinct run that failed only on two flagged sites. The −2 are Sonnet distinct, where Rust's forced JSON arms got wrong content and Python's fallback was right. Change-kind pinning test: +3 (alter). DESCRIBE with an unknown operand: +2 (Opus date). Rust Opus wrote Some(Integer) | None patterns, so the unknown case is a visible value; Python Opus matched DataType values only. This is not compiler-enforced, and n = 3. Silent sites and content: +4. So the compiler's help shows in which sites get reached, not in passes: the weak runs it guides fail elsewhere.
Cost. Output tokens per run are about the same in both languages (Haiku 75k vs 81k, Sonnet 32k vs 36k, Opus 50k vs 49k). Python runs took more turns: Haiku 90 vs 71, Sonnet 53 vs 43.
